newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: High credit growth dampens S.Africa rate cut hopes.
newsitem.headline: High credit growth dampens S.Africa rate cut hopes.

text.p: Continued high private sector credit growth in June has put a dampener on hopes of an imminent cut in South African interest rates, economists said on Monday.

Overall broadly-defined M3 money supply actually dipped in June from May. But the private credit component, which Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals has vowed to bring under control, jumped by nearly eight billion rand.
Long bond yields kicked up after the data was released at 1500 GMT as investors sold stock in the belief that prospects for a rate cut, possibly as early as this week, had faded.
"It is still a possibility for August but this number suggests that we shouldn't get too excited too soon," said Julia Roy, treasury economist at Rand Merchant Bank.
Year-on-year M3 grew 12.79 percent in June from a revised 15.32 in May, well below the Reuters consensus poll of economists which had forecast 14.44 percent.
But private credit dipped only marginally to 16.39 percent from 16.65 in May, against the consensus expectation of 15.19 percent.
Dawie Roodt, economist at Equisec, said the jump in credit growth may have reflected a temporary decision by South African borrowers to repay foreign debts and bring debts back onshore.
Their actions were probably prompted by anxieties about the rand in the run-up to the relaxation of exchange controls on July 1.

"I think a lot of guys got scared and decided to repay foreign loans in June just in case...We could see a reversal in July. The guys might move to offshore funding again and in the process produce a reversal of what happned in June," he said.

That might suggest Stals will wait for another month's money supply data before easing monetary policy. But rate cut hopes could yet be revived on Tuesday when the Central Statistical Services releases June consumer inflation data at 0900 GMT.
Economists expect CPI to continue the trend of the last two months by falling further to 9.1 percent year-on-year compared with May's 9.5 percent rise.

Rate cut speculation has been mounting in South Africa in recent weeks following the successful relaxation of exchange controls on July 1 which failed to trigger the immediate flight of funds some had feared.

Reserve Bank deputy governor Chris de Swardt fuelled the flames at the weekend, telling a Sunday newspaper that the central bank was beginning to see scope for a cut in the key Bank rate from its current level of 17 percent.
